title: Alia Bhatt, Cannes, and India’s Exhausting Need to Be Noticed
excerpt: A viral red-carpet clip, a mother’s defence, and the diaspora’s unresolved relationship with Western validation
body:
A few seconds of footage from the Cannes Film Festival red carpet have, predictably, become the latest battleground in India’s never-ending culture war over celebrity, nationalism, and the aching need for Western approval. In the clip that went viral this week, Alia Bhatt — standing on the famous steps of the Palais des Festivals — appears to pause as photographers briefly turn their cameras elsewhere. Within hours, the internet had rendered its verdict: India’s biggest young star had been “ignored” by the West.

## What Actually Happened

Bhatt, 33, was at Cannes as a global ambassador for L’Oréal Paris, her third appearance at the festival. She walked the red carpet for the premiere of “La Venus Electrique,” wearing a sculpted corseted gown by Tamara Ralph accessorised with Golconda Rose jewelry. Her second look — a pastel mint-green ensemble by designer Yash Patil, styled with a dupatta-inspired trail — drew comparisons to a “Disney princess.” By any professional standard, it was a polished, confident showing.

But the viral clip told a different story. In the chaos of the red carpet — where dozens of celebrities cycle through in quick succession and photographers pivot constantly between subjects — a brief moment of inattention was isolated, amplified, and repackaged as a national humiliation. Social media accounts framed it as proof that Bollywood doesn’t matter on the global stage. Others used it to relitigate older grievances about Bhatt’s privileged background and industry connections.

## Soni Razdan Steps In

Bhatt’s mother, the veteran actress Soni Razdan, responded with a measured but pointed defence. “Social media is full of hate,” she wrote, arguing that the obsession with whether Cannes photographers paid sufficient attention to an Indian star revealed more about Indian insecurities than about Western attitudes. She pointed to the irony of demanding that India be taken seriously on the world stage while simultaneously tearing down the Indians who show up there.

Razdan highlighted what she called a pattern of societal hostility toward successful women — the impulse to find the stumble in every stride, the eagerness to frame achievement as somehow unearned. “More than society, it’s the women who are hardest on other women,” she observed, in a comment that landed with particular force given Bhatt’s history of facing both misogynistic trolling and allegations of nepotism.

Bhatt herself responded with characteristic dry humour. “Why pity, love?” she wrote to one troll. “You noticed me.”

## The Validation Trap

The episode is a case study in what scholars of diaspora identity call the “validation trap” — the double bind in which Indians abroad simultaneously crave recognition from Western institutions and resent themselves for craving it. Cannes, which has no particular obligation to celebrate Bollywood, becomes a proxy for every slight, real or imagined, that Indians have felt on foreign soil.

Bollywood stars Sonu Sood and Aly Goni weighed in with supportive messages, emphasising pride in Bhatt’s presence at the festival. But the broader discourse revealed a fissure: between those who see an Indian actress at Cannes as representation and those who see it as a performance of aspirational proximity to whiteness.

## What NRIs Recognise

For Indians living abroad, the dynamics are uncomfortably familiar. The micro-scrutiny of how you are received in Western spaces — whether the waiter looked at you, whether the colleague mispronounced your name, whether the photographer turned away — is a daily negotiation that most NRIs have internalised so deeply they barely notice it anymore.

What Razdan articulated, perhaps without intending to, is that the trolling of Alia Bhatt is not really about Alia Bhatt. It is about a country still working out whether it wants to be validated by the West or whether it has the confidence to stop keeping score. At Cannes, on social media, and in the lived experience of every Indian who has ever stood in a room wondering if they were being seen — the question remains unresolved.
